extracted.intended_audience: agency counsel, regulated parties, administrative law attorneys, and rulemaking advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal standards for agencies and stakeholders on formulating, publishing, commenting on, and litigating federal administrative rules under the APA and related statutes. Covers notice requirements, recordkeeping, comment practice, types of rulemaking, and judicial review standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness / due process: notice and opportunity to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s all about FAIRNESS! Limiting executive power and preventing 'secret law' — due process: notice & opportunity to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What laws govern the rulemaking at issue? Ensure public is given meaningful notice and chance to submit written data, views or arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Register publication requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Register publication required for agency organization statements, procedures, other information; substantive and procedural rules; statements of general policy; interpretations of general applicability; amendment, revision, or repeal of the foregoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public not bound if agency fails to publish except where there was actual and timely notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOIA access to certain agency materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Available for public inspection and copying: final opinions and orders from adjudications; statements of policy and interpretations not published in FR; administrative staff manuals and instructions to staff that affect a member of the public; index and copies of all FOIA records likely to become subject of subsequent requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use FOIA to obtain record materials; agencies must keep indexes and make certain documents available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a rule and rulemaking types
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency statement of future effect, designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy. Informal Rulemaking (5 U.S.C. § 553) = Notice & comment rulemaking. Formal Rulemaking (5 U.S.C. §§ 556 & 557) = adjudicatory hearing; appropriate for agency fact finding (rare unless statute requires). Hybrid Rulemaking = combination of both; required by some statutes (e.g., OSH Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which rulemaking regime applies based on statute and purpose; use formal only when statute requires or for adjudicatory factfinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard NPRM process
rubrics_metrics.description: NPRM must be published in the Federal Register, public comment taken, final rule published in FR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency may impose additional procedures by statute or executive order or internal practice, but courts may not impose extra procedures (Vermont Yankee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice of proposed rulemaking (ANPRM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency may request comments prior to NPRM. Good way to float novel ideas, narrow or redirect proposal; agencies may also solicit ideas or gather information through less formal means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ANPRM to try out concepts and gather early input; not a substitute for required NPRM if APA requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPRM content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: NPRM must include: legal authority for the rule; either terms or substance of proposed rule or a description of subjects and issues involved. Agency must provide opportunity for public comment and must consider relevant comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure NPRM describes basis and data supporting proposal; omissions can render notice inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful notice and reasonable specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble and regulation text should fairly apprise interested parties of the proposal — meaningful notice and reasonable specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may propose several alternatives and should solicit comments on issues raised; specificity affects whether final action is a logical outgrowth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from APA §553
rubrics_metrics.description: Military or foreign affairs exempt from 553; agency management or personnel matters, public property, loans, grants, benefits, or contracts; interpretive rules, general statements of policy (guidance), or procedural rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm whether a proposed action falls into an exemption before assuming N&C required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause exception to prior notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency finds good cause to skip prior notice and comment if impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. Narrowly construed. Agency must publish good cause statement in the preamble to the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cause must be articulated in the preamble; agencies should be cautious—courts construe narrowly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization: Legislative (substantive) vs Interpretive/Policy/Procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative (substantive) rules are subject to APA N&C procedures. Interpretive rules, statements of policy, procedural rules are subject to publication requirement but not N&C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the rule 'creates new rights or duties' (legislative) or merely 'advises public of agency's interpretation' (interpretive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative rule characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: New law: Creates new rights or duties; modify or add to the legal norm; force and effect of law; binding on all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency action alters legal obligations, it's legislative and requires N&C unless exempted by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rule characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise public of agency’s interpretation of its statutes or regs; do not independently have force and effect of law; legal force derived from underlying law or regulation; do not create new law; not independently enforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive clarifications may avoid N&C but may still have practical effects; courts scrutinize whether a purported interpretive rule actually imposes binding obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance / policy statements: binding question
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the guidance create additional requirements or establish a binding norm? Does the agency retain discretion to apply the guideline or not? Agency practice matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether a guidance functions as a binding norm (legislative) or permits agency discretion (policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rules definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate to agency’s organization, procedures, or practices; do not alter rights or interests of outside parties; do not encode substantial value judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include elimination of expedited approval process, rejection of incomplete application, agency rulemaking procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague statutory language may trigger N&C
rubrics_metrics.description: Some language too vague to be interpreted without N&C procedure (e.g., 'in the public interest', 'just and reasonable', 'fair and equitable', 'as the Secretary deems appropriate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When statutory terms carry broad discretion, agencies should consider N&C to provide clarity and avoid litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment period length (no APA minimum)
rubrics_metrics.description: APA requires opportunity to submit 'written data, views or arguments' but has no required minimum comment period. E.O. 12866 says should be not less than 60 days 'in most cases'; reality often 30 days; 15 day FR Act minimum for public meetings cited in AG Manual as 'a general statutory standard of reasonable notice.' FR notice specifies deadline for comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should set reasonable deadlines; stakeholders can request extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel to seek longer comment periods for complex rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Interested parties may need more time to digest and analyze a complex proposal. Agency decision-making and rationale may benefit from more thoughtful comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request longer periods; agency may grant extensions for complexity, volume, or new issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte communications and agency policies
rubrics_metrics.description: APA does not address permissibility of meetings and other informal contacts before, during or after comment period. 'Ex parte' communications not prohibited in notice and comment rulemaking (Sierra Club v. Costle). Agencies usually have policies regarding such communications based on appearances of impropriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel agency to maintain records of post-comment contacts (agendas, summaries, copies of materials) and to meet with more than one side to avoid appearance issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping of post-comment period contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel agency to maintain record of post-comment period contacts: meeting agendas, summaries, copies of post-comment materials and letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain transparency and administrative record integrity; recordkeeping can help in litigation and response to FOIA requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to write an effective public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain issue clearly and thoroughly; suggest reg text language; use descriptive captions; praise what agency got right; provide independent scientific, legal, and economic impact analyses; offer specific alternatives consistent with rule’s purpose and statutory objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific, documented, actionable input; include analytic support and proposed regulatory text where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for proposed alternatives in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives: Ask for something the agency can actually do. Consider Logical Outgrowth/Scope of the Notice. Would not require statutory change or changes to regs not within scope of NPRM. Suggest standards that are enforceable. Spell out solution that works for your client AND addresses agency’s concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose feasible, enforceable alternatives and give agency basis for final rule conclusions; issues not raised in comments often cannot be raised on judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of a single well-argued comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Not a vote! One well argued and documented comment may serve as the basis for a rulemaking even if thousands of others merely oppose without rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality and reasoning in comments can matter more than number; invest in substantive, documented comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rule preamble requirements (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise general statement of basis and purpose (APA); discussion of changes from the NPRM and why; responses to significant issues; reg text to appear in CFR; Regulatory Impact Statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble should explain agency reasoning and respond to significant comments to survive judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date rules
rubrics_metrics.description: APA: at least 30 days from publication. Exception (shorter): substantive rule granting exemption, relieving restriction; interpretive rule; good cause found by agency and articulated in preamble to final rule. Changing effective date is substantive and requires N&C. Congressional Review Act can delay effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must generally provide 30 days unless a recognized exception applies; changing effective dates post-proposal can trigger N&C requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Final Rule (DFR) use and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Invented by EPA for noncontroversial rules; a final rule effective in X days, UNLESS adverse comments are received within that time. NPRM usually published simultaneously. If adverse comments are received, DFR is rescinded and agency considers comments toward a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DFRs are appropriate for noncontroversial, low-risk rules; agencies must handle adverse comments by rescission and further consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim Final Rule (IFR) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly used if NPRM skipped for good cause. Usually seeks additional, post-promulgation comments. Typically effective upon publication. Reviewable like any other final rule. Can serve as basis of subsequent final rule if original good cause claim was valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IFRs are risky if good cause is weak; agencies should document justification and accept post-promulgation comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction final rule constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: New final rule fixing error(s) in previous final rule. No inherent agency power to correct errors; need to satisfy 'good cause' exception if no NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should rely on good cause and explain why correction without NPRM is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Governs how much the agency can change its mind from NPRM to final rule. Basic rule: no APA violation if final rule is within the scope, and a 'logical outgrowth,' of NPRM. Final rule can be substantially different so long as agency 'fairly apprised' the public of the possibility of changes of the type that occurred. Notice is inadequate if interested parties could not reasonably have anticipated the final rule from the NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether final rule is a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule, not of the comments; if not, agency may need supplemental notice or NODA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must adequately describe and solicit alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies nearly always describe and solicit comment on potential alternatives in preamble to NPRM to select alternative at final rule stage. Whether public 'adequately apprised' often turns on specificity of description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If agency wants to select a new alternative not adequately noticed, it should issue supplemental notice or 'Notice of Data Availability' (NODA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative record scope: 'ALL & ONLY' information
rubrics_metrics.description: ALL & ONLY information the agency relied upon to develop the rule. ALL & ONLY information the court can rely on in judicial review. Agency mostly decides what will be included in the record except for public comments and supporting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build and preserve a complete record; courts are limited to the administrative record for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPRM must describe supporting data and methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: NPRM should describe any data (and any methodology to obtain the data), studies, or assumptions supporting the agency’s proposal. Agency must also make such internal data or studies, along with rest of contents of Administrative Record, publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to make information available before the end of the public comment period = inadequate notice. Agency can add 'supplemental' studies later but should be cautious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Data Availability (NODA)
rubrics_metrics.description: How agencies get comment on new information that becomes available after a comment period closes. Not a second bite at other issues. Can be used for industry-supplied data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NODA to solicit comments on NEW data; avoid using it to reopen substantive issues already closed without proper notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the public docket and reviewing other comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful for private counsel to review record: see what other commenters are saying (rebut? hints as to direction of final rule); may not support agency (useful in commenting or judicial review); 'legislative history' for compliance counseling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All agency dockets are on www.regulations.gov; review early to inform your comment strategy or litigation planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print and maintain copies of internet-cited information
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruct agency to print and maintain copies of any information for which it provides an internet citation in the preamble. Websites frequently change. Printed copies ensure complete rulemaking record and record the date of a website that might change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing web sources in preambles, archive/print to preserve the state of the cited material for the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency articulation of guiding principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage agency to articulate guiding principles for the regulation. Helps agency see forest through the trees, rescues those in the weeds. Principles should be consistent with statutory authority. Policy choices and responses to comments should be consistent with guiding principles. Preamble provides courts and regulated entities guidance and interpretation of reg’s meaning and agency intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear principles improve decision-making coherence and strengthen defensibility in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful review of Regulatory Impact Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Read impact statement carefully — ensure that it accurately characterizes the rule; discrepancies can fuel litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge factual or analytical errors in impact statements during the comment period to avoid later litigation problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition for rulemaking standard and deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Request for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule. Agency decision not to initiate rulemaking is given high level of deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions are often unsuccessful; litigating agency refusal to initiate rulemaking faces a high deference standard (unlawfully withheld only in narrow circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine governing law and venue for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: What law governs? What court? When to file? Sue or intervene? Stay pending complete review? Hurdles to overcome? Standard of review? What if you win?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check statutory judicial review provisions—these may control jurisdiction, venue, and filing windows; where none exist, APA §10 (5 U.S.C. §§701-706) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §706 grounds for review and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Court shall compel agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed; and hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions found to be arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law; contrary to constitutional right; in excess of statutory jurisdiction; without observance of procedure required by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief can include vacatur or remand depending on severity and equities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of judicial review and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: APA creates presumption of judicial review for final agency action not otherwise reviewable. Exceptions: review specifically precluded by statute; actions 'committed to agency discretion by law' (5 U.S.C. §701(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a statutory bar to review applies before filing suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of administrative remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhaustion required? Some statutes specify procedures to be followed before lawsuits can be filed challenging a rule (e.g., CAA §307(d)(7)(B) requires challengers to first file a petition for reconsideration if grounds arose after comment period or it was impracticable to raise then).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statutorily required pre-suit processes (petitions for reconsideration, administrative appeals) to avoid jurisdictional bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory filing windows and publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: APA sets no deadline. General SOL for claims against US is 6 years. Statutory review provisions typically establish jurisdictional filing windows set number of days after 'promulgation'. Note rule deemed published for State Farm purposes when on public display at OFR. Exception: 'grounds arising after'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track OFR posting date and statutory windows; late challenges may be barred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention standards and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Can file complaint (district) or petition (circuit) or intervene in someone else’s case. To intervene must have an interest that could be adversely affected, none of existing parties adequately represent your interest, and be timely. Appeals courts rely on similar criteria as Fed. R. Civ. P. 24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intervention early; intervenors face issues like exclusion from settlements and res judicata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of intervention in support of agency rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Much more difficult to intervene in support of agency rulemaking; standing problems may arise depending on Circuit; doubtful if 'rule' constitutes 'property' or 'transaction' for Rule 24(a) purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters often find intervention procedurally and substantively challenging; anticipate standing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stays and injunctive relief standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency or court can stay rule pending review under APA §705 unless authorizing statute precludes. Temporary Restraining Order & Preliminary Injunction require: likelihood of success on merits; harm to challenger if stay not granted; harm to others if stay is granted; public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to meet all four traditional equitable factors to obtain a stay or PI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final agency action definition (Bennett test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is action 'final'? Bennett v. Spear: action is final if it marks consummation of decisionmaking process and determines rights & obligations; legal consequences flow from it. Court uses pragmatic test (Appalachian Power Co. v. EPA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the agency action has practical legal consequences to determine reviewability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-enforcement review / ripeness (Abbott Laboratories factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-enforcement review permissible if issue is ripe. Two questions: Is the issue 'fit for judicial decision'? (purely legal? sufficiently crystallized?) What is hardship on challenger if review deferred?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If issue is purely legal and hardship is significant, pre-enforcement review may be appropriate; 'window' provisions may cut off collateral challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing doctrine: injury, causation, redressability, and zone of interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional standing requires injury-in-fact, causation, redressability. Also 'zone of interests' test (prudential). Cases matter: Lujan, Summers, Monsanto noted re injury and risk-of-harm analyses; procedural/informational standing considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claimed harms are concrete and imminent; note circuits differ on some standing issues (e.g., informational standing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit differences on intervenor standing and government opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: D.C. Circuit requires intervenors to show standing; Fifth and Eleventh Circuits do not. Government often opposes supporters; results can be lack of standing or lack of interest if only stake is fear of bad precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze relevant circuit law before seeking to intervene in support of or against a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference split: procedures vs substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking procedures: No deference. Substance of rule: Deference to agency interpretations and decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural errors are judged without deference; substantive policy choices receive deference under appropriate standards (Chevron, Auer, Skidmore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron framework for statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the rule consistent with the authorizing statute? Chevron Step 1: Is the statute clear? If so, court applies statute’s clear terms. Chevron Step 2: If statute is unclear, is the agency’s interpretation reasonable? Deference rationale: Congress charged agency with interpreting statute. Brand X: a reasonable agency interpretation trumps prior judicial interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue Step 1 if statute unambiguous; otherwise focus on whether agency interpretation is reasonable under Step 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore and Auer deference distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy statements receive Skidmore 'respect' based on 'power to persuade' (United States v. Mead Corp). Agency’s interpretation of its own rules receives deference (Seminole Rock/Auer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether agency action is a policy/guidance (Skidmore) or an authoritative interpretation of its own regulations (Auer); Auer has been subject to critique and limitation in case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review for violations of other statutes or Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the agency violate some other statute? (NEPA, RFA, Agency’s authorizing statute). Did the agency violate the Constitution? Courts attempt to avoid constitutional questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise statutory compliance claims (NEPA, RFA) where applicable; constitutional claims may be more difficult and avoided by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial scrutiny of agency factfinding and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are highly deferential to agency decision-making. Are fact findings supported by substantial evidence? Did agency articulate a rational connection between facts found and choice made? Did agency respond to significant issues raised in comments? Based upon review of administrative record — not post-hoc rationalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative record must show rational decisionmaking and response to significant comments to survive arbitrary and capricious review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to consider or improper consideration of factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Did agency fail to consider a factor the statute requires? Consider a factor the statute disallows? Depart from prior policies/precedents without explanation? Courts impose same degree of scrutiny to rules changing or rescinding earlier rules (State Farm; FCC v. Fox).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When agency changes course, it must provide reasoned explanation and address reliance interests and prior policy bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies: vacatur versus remand
rubrics_metrics.description: APA 706: 'The reviewing court shall . . . hold unlawful and set aside' agency action found to be arbitrary/capricious, in excess, etc. 'Vacatur' vs. 'Remand' — If court vacates, rule is gone (but remains in effect until court issues 'mandate'). If court remands, rule stays in effect while agency provides additional justification or revises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh equities and consequences when choosing vacatur vs remand; challengers should argue for vacatur if the rule causes substantial harm and cannot stand.
